first_impression.reaction: Typed 'wedding table settings' on the train, half wanting pretty ideas and half wanting to know where the forks go. The opening paragraph is a bit poetic for a phone, but the Key Takeaways answer the 'where does everything go' part in four bullets, so I stayed. What I really wanted was the themed looks, and the takeaways don't tell me they're there or how many there are. I found them by scrolling. Bookmarking it for the theme lists and the FAQ, not enquiring.

journey.quote: A wedding table is built one place at a time. Before the florals arrive and the candles are lit, every guest sits down to the same small arrangement of plate, cutlery, glass, napkin and name card, and that arrangement tells them how the evening will run.
journey.reaction: Nice writing, but it's a mood paragraph. On a phone I'm already scrolling past it to find the answer.

journey.quote: Forks sit to the left, knives and spoons to the right, glasses above the knives, and dessert cutlery either above the plate or brought out with dessert.
journey.reaction: That's the direct answer. Screenshot-able. Good.

journey.quote: A theme lives in the finish of each piece (plate, cutlery, glass, napkin and stationery), not in adding more to the table.
journey.reaction: Fine as an idea, but I wanted to know which themes you actually cover. Nothing here tells me there are seven looks further down.

journey.section: The place setting, piece by piece
journey.quote: Treat them as a well-tested framework rather than a set of Australian rules, and adapt them to your menu.
journey.reaction: I like that they say where the rules come from. Feels honest, not made up.

journey.quote: It can arrive with dessert, or it can sit above the plate for the whole meal, with the fork's handle pointing left and the spoon above it, handle pointing right.
journey.reaction: I had to read this twice. This is the kind of thing I need a picture for, not a sentence.

journey.quote: Below, each theme is translated into the same five choices: plate, cutlery finish, glass, napkin and stationery.
journey.reaction: This is what I came for. Same five bullets per theme makes it easy to compare while scrolling.

journey.quote: **Stationery:** a card weighted with a small stone or shell, so it stays put outdoors.
journey.reaction: Practical little tip I wouldn't have thought of. This is bookmark material.

journey.quote: For tables designers have built around a single idea, browse the [tablescapes from the Table Design Exhibition](https://weddedwonderland.com/table-design-exhibition-2025-theme).
journey.reaction: Probably the link I'd actually tap next, because I want to see these, not just read lists.

journey.section: Table settings for a destination wedding
journey.quote: Abroad, the question is not only which look you love, but which look the venue can actually lay.
journey.reaction: Not my situation right now, so I skimmed. The question list is tidy though.

journey.quote: ### Should the napkin go on the plate or to the left?
journey.reaction: Exactly the sort of question I'd type into Google. Short answer, done.

journey.section: Set the table with someone in your corner
journey.quote: When you are ready to talk through your reception, speak with our [Wedded Concierge](https://weddedwonderland.com/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=22-amazing-table-settings-for-every-wedding-theme&utm_content=closing) team.
journey.reaction: I don't know who you are yet and I came for napkin folds. Not ready to talk to anyone.

turn_offs_found.quote: A wedding table is built one place at a time. Before the florals arrive and the candles are lit, every guest sits down to the same small arrangement of plate, cutlery, glass, napkin and name card, and that arrangement tells them how the evening will run.
turn_offs_found.why: Atmospheric opener before the answer. Not long, but it's the first thing I see on a small screen.

turn_offs_found.quote: A theme lives in the finish of each piece (plate, cutlery, glass, napkin and stationery), not in adding more to the table.
turn_offs_found.why: The theme content is the main reason most people search this, but the takeaways don't name the themes, so I had to scroll through cutlery etiquette and service styles to find them.

turn_offs_found.quote: It can arrive with dessert, or it can sit above the plate for the whole meal, with the fork's handle pointing left and the spoon above it, handle pointing right.
turn_offs_found.why: Spatial directions in words are hard to follow on a phone without a diagram.

would_share_with: My partner: a screenshot of the coastal or garden theme bullets
My maid of honour: the Key Takeaways for the etiquette basics

cta_reaction.quote: If you have a venue in mind and want to know which of these looks it can carry, talk it through with our [Wedded Concierge](https://weddedwonderland.com/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=22-amazing-table-settings-for-every-wedding-theme&utm_content=secondary) team.
cta_reaction.why: Well placed right after the themes, but I'm still browsing ideas, don't know the brand and have no idea if it costs anything. Bookmark, not enquire. I'd tap the Table Design Exhibition link instead.

top_3_changes: Name the themes in the Key Takeaways so a skimmer knows they're on the page. Old: "- A theme lives in the finish of each piece (plate, cutlery, glass, napkin and stationery), not in adding more to the table." New: "- A theme lives in the finish of each piece (plate, cutlery, glass, napkin and stationery), not in adding more to the table. Seven looks are set out below: classic and formal, pared back, garden and romantic, coastal, country estate, winter and candlelit, and playful and retro."

Point theme-hunters straight to the themes in the intro. Old: "This guide to wedding table settings works through each piece in the order it is laid, then shows how a theme changes the same pieces." New: "This guide to wedding table settings works through each piece in the order it is laid, then shows how seven themes change the same pieces. If you are here for ideas, skip to the themes." (link 'skip to the themes' to the 'Wedding table settings by theme' heading anchor)

Make sure the place-setting image slot is filled before publish, and caption it so the dessert cutlery sentence has something to point at. Old: "Dessert cutlery has two options." New: "Dessert cutlery has two options, both shown in the place setting above." (only if the image shows dessert cutlery above the plate, as the slot brief asks)

open_questions.question: The slug promises '22 amazing table settings' but the draft has seven themes. Is the published title/H1 the one in the front matter, so a searcher isn't expecting 22?

assumptions: Priya arrived from a Google search for 'wedding table settings' on her phone, does not know the brand and is browsing ideas rather than planning a destination wedding.
The image slots are treated as unseen; the reaction to the dessert cutlery sentence assumes no diagram is visible at that point.
No prices, fees or supplier details invented; cost and service questions listed as unanswered.
